cues.text: MIT 8111, Ethics and Legal Issues in Information Technology.
Study Session 6: Ethical Dilemmas in Emerging Technologies and Case Studies.
We begin with the first topic: emerging technologies and responsible innovation.
Emerging technologies create new capabilities, and they also create uncertainty.
Let us look at the main ones named in this section, and what each one does.
Artificial intelligence, or AI, supports prediction, classification, generation and decisions.
The Internet of Things, or IoT, connects sensors and devices.
Robotics and automation execute physical and digital tasks.
Blockchain coordinates shared records.
Cloud and edge computing provide scalable or local computation; cloud for scale, edge for computation done locally.
And immersive technologies and advanced analytics change the way people interact with systems and with one another.
Now, why does this matter for ethics?
Because each of these capabilities brings both promise and danger, and we need to weigh them together.
First, the benefits.
The source lists efficiency, healthcare access, predictive maintenance, safer operations, resource optimisation, personalised services, and new business models.
Second, the risks.
These include surveillance, discrimination, job displacement, cybersecurity, exclusion, misinformation, opacity, dependence, and concentration of power.
Notice that the same technology can sit on both lists.
A system that personalises services may also watch people closely.
A system that automates tasks may also displace jobs.
Here is a key principle to hold onto: technical novelty does not establish social benefit.
In other words, a technology being new, clever or powerful does not, on its own, prove that it is good for society.
That has to be shown by looking at its effects.
This leads to the idea of responsible innovation.
Responsible innovation does four things.
It evaluates intended and unintended effects, so we ask not only what the technology is designed to do, but what else it might do.
It involves affected stakeholders, meaning the people who will be touched by the technology get a voice.
It anticipates risks, thinking ahead rather than reacting afterwards.
And it adapts to evidence, so that when real-world results show a problem, the approach changes.
Let us now apply this to a concrete setting: Industry 4.0.
Industry 4.0 integrates cyber-physical systems, IoT, real-time analytics, automation and connected production.
Think of a factory where physical machines and digital systems are tied together.
Here is the sequence the source describes.
First, a sensor detects machinery conditions.
Second, analytics predicts failure.
Third, maintenance schedules change based on evidence.
So instead of repairing a machine only after it breaks, or servicing it on a fixed calendar regardless of its state, the maintenance is driven by what the data shows.
This is the predictive maintenance we met in the list of benefits.
The source then turns to supply chains.
Supply-chain visibility can improve inventory and routing.
But the same pervasive tracking can also monitor workers, or expose sensitive commercial data.
So one capability produces a benefit and a risk side by side: better logistics on one hand, worker monitoring and exposure of confidential business information on the other.
So what should we assess when we evaluate such a system?
The source gives us four things: human safety, workforce rights, resilience and oversight.
Is it safe for people?
Does it respect the rights of workers?
Can the system withstand failure or disruption?
And is there meaningful human oversight of how it operates?

Those four questions, together with the habit of evaluating intended and unintended effects, involving stakeholders, anticipating risks and adapting to evidence, are the foundation for the case studies that follow in this study session.
